title: October 17, 2017
insights: Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, as defined in the page’s footnote, to rise from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E. The forecast assigns the category $302 billion in growth and a 4.1% CAGR for 2017E–2021E, compared with approximately 3% for global GDP. Among the three listed revenue segments, Cost of Internet access—including fixed broadband, wireless, and mobile Internet access—is forecast to have the largest dollar increase ($128B) and highest CAGR (5.7%).

In the U.S. in 2017, the top 25% of users with 4.5+ hours of daily video attention accounted for 61% of total video time spent and 34% of total consumer spend. All other users accounted for 39% of video time spent and 66% of consumer spend.

In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, were reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours; Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, were reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours. Separately, in the U.S. in 2017, 31% of sports viewers (more than five hours of sports programming per week) cited Broadcast as a cord-cutter substitution option and 21% cited Virtual Pay TV; among non-sports viewers (no sports programming on a regular basis), the respective shares were 21% and 15% (Activate study, n=1,172).

Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E; the consumer adoption chart measures users as a percentage of global population over 2016–2021E and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The page lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption. The page does not numerically define the threshold for “scaled” adoption.
In 2017, news readers in each of the five selected countries reported a higher perceived-trustworthiness share for News Media than for Social Media.

editorial_plan.report_thesis: Activate pairs a forecast of global consumer Internet and media revenue growth with evidence that audience attention, distribution choices, and adoption conditions differ across media and commerce categories.

themes.theme: Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, as defined in the page’s footnote, to rise from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E, with $302 billion in growth and a 4.1% CAGR; within the three listed revenue segments, Cost of Internet access, including fixed broadband, wireless, and mobile Internet access, is forecast to have the largest dollar increase ($128B) and highest CAGR (5.7%). The page compares the overall revenue CAGR with approximately 3% for global GDP.

In the U.S. in 2017, the top 25% of users with 4.5+ hours of daily video attention accounted for 61% of total video time spent and 34% of total consumer spend; all other users accounted for 39% of video time and 66% of consumer spend. The shares show that video attention and consumer spend are distributed differently across these cohorts.

Sports findings give two distinct audience signals: in Activate’s 2017 study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, were 27% of fans and 61% of hours; separately, in the U.S. in 2017, a higher share of sports viewers than Virtual Pay TV viewers cited Broadcast as a cord-cutter substitution option (31% vs. 21%), as did non-sports viewers (21% vs. 15%).

Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E; the cited barriers are limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area. The forecast is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles, and the page does not numerically define “scaled” adoption.

In 2017, among news readers in five selected countries, the share reporting perceived trustworthiness was higher for News Media than for Social Media: Canada 51% vs. 24%, Ireland 47% vs. 28%, the United Kingdom 41% vs. 18%, Australia 40% vs. 27%, and the United States 38% vs. 20%.

The U.S. eCommerce growth matrix places grocery and automotive in the delayed eCommerce adoption area alongside products involving first-hand experience, with food freshness and used-car condition as examples. It positions categories by 2016 category share of eCommerce sales and potential shift from physical to eCommerce, not by a measured time-to-adoption.

Podcast survey responses distinguish potential listening factors by audience: in Activate’s 2017 study, 34% of podcast non-listeners (n=700) selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to listening, while 31% of podcast listeners (n=419) selected “Recommendations” as a factor that would lead to increased consumption. The page does not specify geography.

key_figures.source_statement: Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, as defined in the page’s footnote, to increase from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E (USD), with $302 billion in growth and a 4.1% CAGR; the page compares this with a global GDP CAGR of approximately 3%.
key_figures.why_it_matters: Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, as defined in the page’s footnote, to rise from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E. The forecast assigns the category $302 billion in growth and a 4.1% CAGR for 2017E–2021E, compared with approximately 3% for global GDP. Among the three listed revenue segments, Cost of Internet access—including fixed broadband, wireless, and mobile Internet access—is forecast to have the largest dollar increase ($128B) and highest CAGR (5.7%).

key_figures.source_statement: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, are reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours. Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, are reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours.
key_figures.why_it_matters: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, were reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours; Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, were reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours. Separately, in the U.S. in 2017, 31% of sports viewers (more than five hours of sports programming per week) cited Broadcast as a cord-cutter substitution option and 21% cited Virtual Pay TV; among non-sports viewers (no sports programming on a regular basis), the respective shares were 21% and 15% (Activate study, n=1,172).

key_figures.figure: News Media exceeded Social Media in all five selected countries
key_figures.label: Perceived trustworthiness by news source, % of news readers
key_figures.metric_public_copy: In 2017, among news readers, perceived trustworthiness for News Media versus Social Media was 51% versus 24% in Canada, 47% versus 28% in Ireland, 41% versus 18% in the United Kingdom, 40% versus 27% in Australia, and 38% versus 20% in the United States.
key_figures.geography: Canada, Ireland, United Kingdom, Australia, United States
key_figures.subject: Perceived trustworthiness by news source
key_figures.source_statement: In 2017, among news readers in the five selected countries, the share reporting perceived trustworthiness was higher for News Media than for Social Media: Canada 51% vs. 24%, Ireland 47% vs. 28%, the United Kingdom 41% vs. 18%, Australia 40% vs. 27%, and the United States 38% vs. 20%.
key_figures.why_it_matters: In 2017, news readers in each of the five selected countries reported a higher perceived-trustworthiness share for News Media than for Social Media.

chart_insight_cards.caption: Consumer Internet and Media Revenues; growth dollars; CAGR
chart_insight_cards.takeaway: Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, as defined in the page’s footnote, to rise from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E. The forecast assigns the category $302 billion in growth and a 4.1% CAGR for 2017E–2021E, compared with approximately 3% for global GDP. Among the three listed revenue segments, Cost of Internet access—including fixed broadband, wireless, and mobile Internet access—is forecast to have the largest dollar increase ($128B) and highest CAGR (5.7%).

chart_insight_cards.takeaway: In the U.S. in 2017, the top 25% of users with 4.5+ hours of daily video attention accounted for 61% of total video time spent and 34% of total consumer spend. All other users accounted for 39% of video time spent and 66% of consumer spend.

chart_insight_cards.caption: Fan-segment share of fans and share of hours
chart_insight_cards.takeaway: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, were reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours; Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, were reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours. Separately, in the U.S. in 2017, 31% of sports viewers (more than five hours of sports programming per week) cited Broadcast as a cord-cutter substitution option and 21% cited Virtual Pay TV; among non-sports viewers (no sports programming on a regular basis), the respective shares were 21% and 15% (Activate study, n=1,172).
chart_insight_cards.public_takeaway: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, were reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours; Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, were reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours. Separately, in the U.S. in 2017, 31% of sports viewers (more than five hours of sports programming per week) cited Broadcast as a cord-cutter substitution option and 21% cited Virtual Pay TV; among non-sports viewers (no sports programming on a regular basis), the respective shares were 21% and 15% (Activate study, n=1,172).
chart_insight_cards.business_implication: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, were reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours; Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, were reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours. Separately, in the U.S. in 2017, 31% of sports viewers (more than five hours of sports programming per week) cited Broadcast as a cord-cutter substitution option and 21% cited Virtual Pay TV; among non-sports viewers (no sports programming on a regular basis), the respective shares were 21% and 15% (Activate study, n=1,172).

chart_insight_cards.caption: Factors that would lead to podcast listening / increased podcast consumption
chart_insight_cards.takeaway: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study, 34% of podcast non-listeners (n=700) selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to podcast listening. Separately, 31% of podcast listeners (n=419) selected “Recommendations” as a factor that would lead to increased podcast consumption.

summary.executive_summary: Activate forecasts footnote-defined global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues to rise from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E, with $302 billion growth and a 4.1% CAGR versus approximately 3% for global GDP. Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues at $2.0 trillion in 2021E. In Activate’s global 2017E–2021E forecast, Cost of Internet access, including fixed broadband, wireless, and mobile Internet access, is projected to increase by $128B, the largest dollar increase among the three listed revenue segments, and to have the highest CAGR at 5.7%. In the U.S. in 2017, the top 25% of users with 4.5+ hours of daily video attention accounted for 61% of total video time spent and 34% of total consumer spend, while all other users accounted for 39% of video time spent and 66% of consumer spend. In Activate’s 2017 study, 34% of podcast non-listeners (n=700) selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to podcast listening.

insights_candidates.text: Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E. The page’s global consumer VR adoption chart measures users as a percentage of population, spans 2016–2021E, and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The chart labels the Mobile VR series with a footnote excluding Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers. It lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption.

source_truth_notes_by_page.42: The page headline forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption. Its chart title specifies consumer VR adoption globally over 2016–2021E as a percentage of population, and the y-axis specifies users as a percentage of global population. Footnote 1 identifies the seventh-generation gaming-console modeling basis. The “Mobile VR²” series label is attached to the mobile line, and footnote 2 excludes Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers from that series. The mass-adoption barriers box lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area. The timeline marks 2016 without E and the 2017–2021 estimates with E.

verified_fact.statement: The U.S. eCommerce growth matrix groups grocery and automotive with products involving first-hand experience, giving food freshness and used-car condition as examples, and places them in the delayed eCommerce adoption area. The matrix positions categories by 2016 category share of eCommerce sales and potential shift from physical to eCommerce; it does not report a measured time-to-adoption.
qualifiers: The chart is for the U.S.
The horizontal axis is category share of eCommerce sales in 2016; the vertical axis is potential for shift from physical to eCommerce, shown qualitatively from low to high.
The first-hand-experience callout gives food freshness and used-car condition as examples and points to the area containing grocery and automotive.
Delayed eCommerce adoption is a qualitative chart grouping, not a measured duration or time-to-adoption.

source_truth_notes_by_page.119: The chart is titled “Ecommerce Growth Potential by Category, U.S.” Its horizontal axis specifies category share of eCommerce sales in 2016, and its vertical axis specifies potential for shift from physical to eCommerce, with low-to-high positioning. The callout “Products involve first-hand experience (e.g. food freshness, used car condition)” points to the chart region containing grocery and automotive; that region is labeled “Delayed Ecommerce Adoption.” These are qualitative category placements, not a time-to-adoption measure.

insights_final.text: Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, as defined in the page’s footnote, to rise from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E. The forecast assigns the category $302 billion in growth and a 4.1% CAGR for 2017E–2021E, compared with approximately 3% for global GDP. Among the three listed revenue segments, Cost of Internet access—including fixed broadband, wireless, and mobile Internet access—is forecast to have the largest dollar increase ($128B) and highest CAGR (5.7%).

insights_final.text: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, were reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours; Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, were reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours. Separately, in the U.S. in 2017, 31% of sports viewers (more than five hours of sports programming per week) cited Broadcast as a cord-cutter substitution option and 21% cited Virtual Pay TV; among non-sports viewers (no sports programming on a regular basis), the respective shares were 21% and 15% (Activate study, n=1,172).

insights_final.text: Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E; the consumer adoption chart measures users as a percentage of global population over 2016–2021E and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The page lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption. The page does not numerically define the threshold for “scaled” adoption.

insights_final.text: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study, 34% of podcast non-listeners (n=700) selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to podcast listening. insights_final.so_what: The survey distinguishes an access-navigation factor among non-listeners from a recommendation factor among current listeners.
insights_final.now_what: MarketLense recommendation: Test app-discovery messaging with non-listeners and recommendation prompts with listeners, measuring each group separately.
insights_final.metric_public_copy: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study, 34% of podcast non-listeners (n=700) selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to podcast listening.

artifacts.expert_comment: Podcast survey responses distinguish audience stages: among non-listeners, 34% selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to listening (n=700); among listeners, 31% selected “Recommendations” as a factor that would lead to increased consumption (n=419). Separately, the U.S. eCommerce matrix places grocery and automotive in its delayed-adoption area alongside products involving first-hand experience, while positioning categories by 2016 eCommerce sales share and potential shift from physical to eCommerce, not by a measured adoption timetable. Together, the findings point to a decision-design tension: the relevant diagnostic differs by audience stage in podcasts and by product category in eCommerce, so a single adoption label or intervention would blur distinctions the evidence makes. MarketLense would recommend, where these areas are in scope, assessing podcast listening and increased consumption separately and treating the eCommerce matrix as category positioning rather than timing guidance.

claim_ledgers.claim_text: Activate forecasts footnote-defined global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues to rise from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E, with $302 billion growth and a 4.1% CAGR versus approximately 3% for global GDP.
Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues at $2.0 trillion in 2021E.

In Activate’s global 2017E–2021E forecast, Cost of Internet access, including fixed broadband, wireless, and mobile Internet access, is projected to increase by $128B, the largest dollar increase among the three listed revenue segments, and to have the highest CAGR at 5.7%.

In the U.S. in 2017, the top 25% of users with 4.5+ hours of daily video attention accounted for 61% of total video time spent and 34% of total consumer spend, while all other users accounted for 39% of video time spent and 66% of consumer spend.
In Activate’s 2017 study, 34% of podcast non-listeners (n=700) selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to podcast listening.

Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, as defined in the page’s footnote, to rise from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E. The forecast assigns the category $302 billion in growth and a 4.1% CAGR for 2017E–2021E, compared with approximately 3% for global GDP. Among the three listed revenue segments, Cost of Internet access—including fixed broadband, wireless, and mobile Internet access—is forecast to have the largest dollar increase ($128B) and highest CAGR (5.7%).

In the U.S. in 2017, the top 25% of users with 4.5+ hours of daily video attention accounted for 61% of total video time spent and 34% of total consumer spend. All other users accounted for 39% of video time spent and 66% of consumer spend.

In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, were reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours; Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, were reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours. Separately, in the U.S. in 2017, 31% of sports viewers (more than five hours of sports programming per week) cited Broadcast as a cord-cutter substitution option and 21% cited Virtual Pay TV; among non-sports viewers (no sports programming on a regular basis), the respective shares were 21% and 15% (Activate study, n=1,172).

Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E; the consumer adoption chart measures users as a percentage of global population over 2016–2021E and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The page lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption. The page does not numerically define the threshold for “scaled” adoption.
In 2017, news readers in each of the five selected countries reported a higher perceived-trustworthiness share for News Media than for Social Media.

The U.S. eCommerce growth matrix places grocery and automotive in its “Delayed Ecommerce Adoption” area alongside products involving first-hand experience, with food freshness and used-car condition as examples. It positions categories by 2016 category share of eCommerce sales and potential shift from physical to eCommerce; these are qualitative placements, not a measured time-to-adoption.

In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study, 34% of podcast non-listeners (n=700) selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to podcast listening. Separately, 31% of podcast listeners (n=419) selected “Recommendations” as a factor that would lead to increased podcast consumption.

findings.text: The U.S. eCommerce growth matrix groups grocery and automotive with products involving first-hand experience, giving food freshness and used-car condition as examples, and places them in the delayed eCommerce adoption area. The matrix positions categories by 2016 category share of eCommerce sales and potential shift from physical to eCommerce; it does not report a measured time-to-adoption.

findings.text: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, are reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours. Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, are reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours.

verified_facts.statement: Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E. The page’s global consumer VR adoption chart measures users as a percentage of population, spans 2016–2021E, and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The chart labels the Mobile VR series with a footnote excluding Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers. It lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption.
qualifiers: The chart shows 2016 without an E and labels 2017E–2021E as estimates.
The cardboard-viewer exclusion applies specifically to the Mobile VR series, not all VR adoption.
The page does not numerically define the threshold for “scaled” adoption.

source_truth_notes_by_page.42: The page headline forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption. Its chart title specifies consumer VR adoption globally over 2016–2021E as a percentage of population, and the y-axis specifies users as a percentage of global population. Footnote 1 identifies the seventh-generation gaming-console modeling basis. The “Mobile VR²” series label is attached to the mobile line, and footnote 2 excludes Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers from that series. The mass-adoption barriers box lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area. The timeline marks 2016 without E and the 2017–2021 estimates with E.

evidence_spans.text: The page headline forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption. Its chart title specifies consumer VR adoption globally over 2016–2021E as a percentage of population, and the y-axis specifies users as a percentage of global population. Footnote 1 identifies the seventh-generation gaming-console modeling basis. The “Mobile VR²” series label is attached to the mobile line, and footnote 2 excludes Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers from that series. The mass-adoption barriers box lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area. The timeline marks 2016 without E and the 2017–2021 estimates with E.

planned_themes: Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, as defined in the page’s footnote, to rise from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E, with $302 billion in growth and a 4.1% CAGR; within the three listed revenue segments, Cost of Internet access, including fixed broadband, wireless, and mobile Internet access, is forecast to have the largest dollar increase ($128B) and highest CAGR (5.7%). The page compares the overall revenue CAGR with approximately 3% for global GDP.

In the U.S. in 2017, the top 25% of users with 4.5+ hours of daily video attention accounted for 61% of total video time spent and 34% of total consumer spend; all other users accounted for 39% of video time and 66% of consumer spend. The shares show that video attention and consumer spend are distributed differently across these cohorts.

Sports findings give two distinct audience signals: in Activate’s 2017 study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, were 27% of fans and 61% of hours; separately, in the U.S. in 2017, a higher share of sports viewers than Virtual Pay TV viewers cited Broadcast as a cord-cutter substitution option (31% vs. 21%), as did non-sports viewers (21% vs. 15%).

Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E; the cited barriers are limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area. The forecast is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles, and the page does not numerically define “scaled” adoption.

In 2017, among news readers in five selected countries, the share reporting perceived trustworthiness was higher for News Media than for Social Media: Canada 51% vs. 24%, Ireland 47% vs. 28%, the United Kingdom 41% vs. 18%, Australia 40% vs. 27%, and the United States 38% vs. 20%.

The U.S. eCommerce growth matrix places grocery and automotive in the delayed eCommerce adoption area alongside products involving first-hand experience, with food freshness and used-car condition as examples. It positions categories by 2016 category share of eCommerce sales and potential shift from physical to eCommerce, not by a measured time-to-adoption.

Podcast survey responses distinguish potential listening factors by audience: in Activate’s 2017 study, 34% of podcast non-listeners (n=700) selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to listening, while 31% of podcast listeners (n=419) selected “Recommendations” as a factor that would lead to increased consumption. The page does not specify geography.

doc_map.title: Activate Technology & Media Outlook 2018
doc_map.summary: Activate’s outlook surveys major technology, media, and consumer trends shaping the year ahead. It combines consumer research, market analysis, and forecasts across media attention and spending, smart speakers and reality computing, online video, premium video, sports, news, eCommerce, and podcasts; its opening letter describes analysis based on proprietary research and large-scale U.S. population surveys.

sections.title: $300 Billion in Tech and Media Growth Dollars
sections.summary: The opening outlook quantifies forecast growth in global consumer Internet and media revenues. It compares the projected growth rate with global GDP and breaks out expected sources of revenue growth.
key_points: The chart “Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, Global, 2017E–2021E” forecasts growth from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E, or $302 billion; the displayed CAGR is 4.1% versus approximately 3% for global GDP (p. 4).
The following segment chart presents revenue growth by paid content, advertising, and Internet access, with 2017E–2021E comparisons (p. 5).

sections.title: There are 31 Hours in a Day
sections.summary: This section examines how consumers allocate attention across technology and media activities, framing the total as a day that can exceed 24 hours when media use overlaps. It considers the implications of that attention landscape for media and technology businesses.
key_points: The section frames combined media attention as extending beyond a conventional 24-hour day.
The report’s introduction identifies consumer time allocation as one of the outlook’s forecast topics.

sections.title: Super Users: A Lot More Time, a Lot More Money
sections.summary: The section compares high-attention consumers with other users, showing that the most engaged groups account for disproportionately large shares of media time and spending. It includes separate video and audio comparisons.
key_points: In “Video Time and Spend Relative to Share of Users,” U.S., 2017, the top 25% of users—those with 4.5+ hours of daily video attention—account for 61% of video time and 34% of consumer spend (p. 14).
In “Audio Time and Spend Relative to Share of Users,” U.S., 2017, the top 25%—those with 3+ hours of daily audio attention—account for 64% of audio time and 47% of consumer spend (p. 16).

sections.title: Smart Speaker Battles are about the Great Digital Assistant Wars
sections.summary: The section treats smart speakers as an entry point in a broader competition to own digital assistants and their conversational interface. It describes the strategic stakes for technology companies, the falling cost of access, and the early uses of smart speakers.
key_points: The report describes dedicated smart speakers as a “trojan horse” for bringing AI and digital assistants into the home; it expects assistant access to become ubiquitous across devices (p. 22).
The chart “Entry Price Points for Digital Assistant-Enabled Devices,” U.S., 2014–2017, shows the access price moving from $180 in 2014 to free in 2017 (p. 26).
Smart-speaker owners primarily use the devices for music and a limited set of portal functions, including questions, weather, alarms, news, directions, and time checks (p. 29).

sections.title: Reality Computing: VR/AR Move from Entertainment to the Next Big Computing Platform
sections.summary: The report traces virtual and augmented reality from primarily entertainment uses toward a broader computing platform integrating digital and physical environments. It presents adoption and spending forecasts, along with possible consumer and enterprise applications.
key_points: The chart “Consumer and Enterprise Spend on VR/AR,” Global, 2016–2021E, forecasts a $71 billion Reality Computing business in 2021 (p. 37).
The report forecasts that consumer VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021, citing limited applications beyond gaming, limited social use, and restricted movement (p. 41).
It argues that AR-enabled smartphones can bring the technology to large audiences, while enterprise applications include workflow support and worker collaboration (pp. 42–46).

sections.title: Big Influencers and Media Brands will Rule Web Video
sections.summary: This section examines the concentration of web-video views among top creators and the roles of influencers and media companies across YouTube and Facebook. It also considers the content categories and creators that attract audiences.
key_points: In “Share of Top YouTube and Facebook Creators vs. Share of Views by Platform,” Global, Q2 2017, creators with 50M+ total views comprise 24% of the selected YouTube creators and account for 71% of views; on Facebook, they comprise 26% and account for 77% of views (p. 52).
Among top creators with over 50M views in Q2 2017, influencers account for 83% of YouTube views and media companies 17%; on Facebook, the split is 52% influencers and 48% media companies (p. 53).
The report identifies TV shows, artists, and TV networks among leading U.S. media-company creators on YouTube (p. 55).

sections.title: Premium Video: The Chase for Television Viewers and Television Dollars
sections.summary: The section examines competition among traditional television, virtual pay TV, subscription video, and other viewing options for audiences and revenue. It emphasizes the continuing appeal of live and linear programming, particularly sports, as viewing and distribution choices change.
key_points: In “Cord-Cutter Substitution by Viewer Type,” U.S., 2017, broadcast is presented as more attractive than virtual pay TV for cord-cutters who still want low-cost live or linear programming such as sports (p. 69).
The companion chart “OTA Broadcast-Only Homes,” U.S., 2012–2017E, shows households increasing from 11.2 million in 2012 to 15.8 million in 2017E, a 41% rise (p. 69).

sections.title: Sports is the Ultimate Moat
sections.summary: The report considers sports a durable source of audiences and value for live television, while examining fan segments, viewing platforms, emerging sports, and competition for content rights. It distinguishes highly engaged fans from those who watch mainly for social reasons.
key_points: In the U.S., 2017, 90% of sports viewers say they watch specifically for sports content, while 10% watch only as a social activity (p. 81).
In the U.S., 2017, Super Fans make up 27% of fans but account for 61% of sports-viewing hours; Social Fans make up 10% of fans and 6% of hours (p. 83).
In the U.S., 2017, 62% of eSports viewers are ages 18–34, compared with 30% of traditional sports viewers (p. 89).
The report forecasts that traditional sports revenue in the U.S. will rise from $65.1 billion in 2017E to $74.6 billion in 2021E, with sports-rights revenue growing at a 4.8% CAGR (p. 85).

sections.title: News Brands will Beat Fake News (Spread by Fake Friends)
sections.summary: This section weighs social platforms’ growing role in news discovery against the durability and trust of established news brands. It also addresses publishers’ relationships with platforms, distribution choices, and differences among news consumers.
key_points: In “Sources of News Discovery,” U.S., 2017, social media is cited by 40% of adults and direct visits by 38%; among active news readers searching for news, direct visits lead at 49% versus 33% for social media (p. 97).

In “Perceived Trustworthiness by News Source,” selected countries, 2017, news media scores higher than social media in all five shown countries: Canada 51% vs. 24%, Ireland 47% vs. 28%, United Kingdom 41% vs. 18%, Australia 40% vs. 27%, and United States 38% vs. 20% (p. 100).
The report argues that social platforms need relationships with credible news brands to remain reliable news sources (p. 100).

sections.title: eCommerce: More than Two Trillion Dollars To Go
sections.summary: The section surveys the remaining opportunity in eCommerce, comparing categories by online-sales share and projected adoption. It discusses how consumer preferences and the need for first-hand experience can affect the pace of online adoption across categories.
key_points: The category analysis plots 2016 eCommerce sales share against projected speed of adoption, distinguishing faster- and slower-adopting categories (pp. 118–119).
The report identifies products requiring first-hand experience, such as food freshness or used-car condition, as examples associated with delayed eCommerce adoption (p. 118).

sections.title: In an Era of Voice Control, Look to Podcasting to Engage Users
sections.summary: The final major section examines podcast audience and advertising growth, discovery barriers, listening contexts, and the relationship between podcasts and smart speakers. It also describes podcasts as a source of audience engagement and potential programming development.
key_points: In “Podcast Ad Revenue and Listeners,” U.S., 2014–2021E, the report forecasts podcast advertising revenue rising from $237 million in 2017E to $642 million in 2021E, while listening among the 12+ population is charted over the same period (p. 135).

Among U.S. podcast non-listeners in 2017, 34% identify knowing which apps to use as a factor that would lead them to listen; among listeners, 31% identify recommendations as a factor that would increase consumption (p. 128).
The report says smart-speaker owners are about 1.6 times more likely to listen to podcasts than non-owners, and notes that connected cars and smart speakers may spur listening (p. 126).
Fan-produced podcasts can extend engagement with entertainment franchises; the report gives the example of “Star Wars Minute,” which it says receives 100,000+ weekly downloads (p. 129).

scope.scope: The report covers technology and media trends for 2018, including digital growth and media use, smart speakers and digital assistants, VR/AR, web and premium video, sports, news, eCommerce, and podcasting. Geographic coverage varies across analyses, with U.S. and global data; periods include historical data and forecasts, including 2017–2021.

methods: The report presents Activate analysis and forecasts; specific forecast methods are not described.
Consumer research draws on Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study, with chart-specific samples reported as n=4,047, n=2,406, and n=820.
Some eCommerce adoption measures are indexed from measured consumer preferences in the 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=4,047).
Top news sites were selected from comScore’s Top 100 digital news properties; counts include desktop and mobile sites.
For a YouTube creator analysis, each channel is treated as a unique creator.
The influencer list was Forbes’ Top 10 Influencers list, generated with Traackr and Captiv8 using reach, virality, engagement, earnings per post, outside endorsements, and reputation.
Analyses cite secondary sources including Alexa, comScore, and other topic-specific sources; no validation method is reported.

limitations: Top news sites are selected from comScore’s Top 100 digital news properties; reported site numbers cover desktop and mobile only.

report_context.title: October 17, 2017
report_context.overview: Activate Technology & Media Outlook 2018 by Activate Activate’s outlook surveys major technology, media, and consumer trends shaping the year ahead. It combines consumer research, market analysis, and forecasts across media attention and spending, smart speakers and reality computing, online video, premium video, sports, news, eCommerce, and podcasts; its opening letter describes analysis based on proprietary research and large-scale U.S. population surveys. The report covers technology and media trends for 2018, including digital growth and media use, smart speakers and digital assistants, VR/AR, web and premium video, sports, news, eCommerce, and podcasting. Geographic coverage varies across analyses, with U.S. and global data; periods include historical data and forecasts, including 2017–2021.
methods: The report presents Activate analysis and forecasts; specific forecast methods are not described.
Consumer research draws on Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study, with chart-specific samples reported as n=4,047, n=2,406, and n=820.
Some eCommerce adoption measures are indexed from measured consumer preferences in the 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=4,047).
Top news sites were selected from comScore’s Top 100 digital news properties; counts include desktop and mobile sites.
key_findings: Activate forecasts that global consumer Internet and media revenues will grow by $302 billion from 2017E to 2021E, with a 4.1% CAGR versus approximately 3% for global GDP.
In Activate’s 2017E–2021E global forecast, cost of Internet access has the largest listed segment growth, at $128 billion and a 5.7% CAGR.
In the United States in 2017, the top 25% of video users, defined as having 4.5+ hours of daily video attention, accounted for 61% of video time.
In the United States in 2017, the top 25% of video users, defined as having 4.5+ hours of daily video attention, accounted for 34% of consumer spend.
Activate expects dedicated smart speakers to serve as a “trojan horse” for delivering AI into the home and expects digital assistants to become ubiquitous across a broad set of devices.
Activate forecasts that consumer VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E, citing limited applications outside gaming, limited social use, and confinement that restricts movement.
limitations: Top news sites are selected from comScore’s Top 100 digital news properties; reported site numbers cover desktop and mobile only.
The report notes that “Mixed Reality” is defined inconsistently by technology and media companies, and is sometimes used to describe VR.
AR-optimized smartphones are defined as phones with 6DoF tracking enabled by SLAM, which requires carefully calibrated hardware and software.
The AR enterprise-market examples cover three major early applications; the report notes that other industries may also be affected.

sections.section_label: $300 Billion in Tech and Media Growth Dollars
sections.summary: The opening outlook quantifies forecast growth in global consumer Internet and media revenues. It compares the projected growth rate with global GDP and breaks out expected sources of revenue growth.
key_points: The chart “Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, Global, 2017E–2021E” forecasts growth from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E, or $302 billion; the displayed CAGR is 4.1% versus appr...
The following segment chart presents revenue growth by paid content, advertising, and Internet access, with 2017E–2021E comparisons (p. 5).

sections.section_label: There are 31 Hours in a Day
sections.summary: This section examines how consumers allocate attention across technology and media activities, framing the total as a day that can exceed 24 hours when media use overlaps. It considers the implications of that attention landscape for media and technology bu...
key_points: The section frames combined media attention as extending beyond a conventional 24-hour day.
The report’s introduction identifies consumer time allocation as one of the outlook’s forecast topics.

sections.section_label: Super Users: A Lot More Time, a Lot More Money
sections.summary: The section compares high-attention consumers with other users, showing that the most engaged groups account for disproportionately large shares of media time and spending. It includes separate video and audio comparisons.
key_points: In “Video Time and Spend Relative to Share of Users,” U.S., 2017, the top 25% of users—those with 4.5+ hours of daily video attention—account for 61% of video time and 34% of consumer spend (p. 14).
In “Audio Time and Spend Relative to Share of Users,” U.S., 2017, the top 25%—those with 3+ hours of daily audio attention—account for 64% of audio time and 47% of consumer spend (p. 16).

sections.section_label: Smart Speaker Battles are about the Great Digital Assistant Wars
sections.summary: The section treats smart speakers as an entry point in a broader competition to own digital assistants and their conversational interface. It describes the strategic stakes for technology companies, the falling cost of access, and the early uses of smart sp...
key_points: The report describes dedicated smart speakers as a “trojan horse” for bringing AI and digital assistants into the home; it expects assistant access to become ubiquitous across devices (p. 22).
The chart “Entry Price Points for Digital Assistant-Enabled Devices,” U.S., 2014–2017, shows the access price moving from $180 in 2014 to free in 2017 (p. 26).
Smart-speaker owners primarily use the devices for music and a limited set of portal functions, including questions, weather, alarms, news, directions, and time checks (p. 29).

sections.section_label: Reality Computing: VR/AR Move from Entertainment to the Next Big Computing Platform
sections.summary: The report traces virtual and augmented reality from primarily entertainment uses toward a broader computing platform integrating digital and physical environments. It presents adoption and spending forecasts, along with possible consumer and enterprise app...
key_points: The chart “Consumer and Enterprise Spend on VR/AR,” Global, 2016–2021E, forecasts a $71 billion Reality Computing business in 2021 (p. 37).
The report forecasts that consumer VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021, citing limited applications beyond gaming, limited social use, and restricted movement (p. 41).
It argues that AR-enabled smartphones can bring the technology to large audiences, while enterprise applications include workflow support and worker collaboration (pp. 42–46).

sections.section_label: Big Influencers and Media Brands will Rule Web Video
sections.summary: This section examines the concentration of web-video views among top creators and the roles of influencers and media companies across YouTube and Facebook. It also considers the content categories and creators that attract audiences.
key_points: In “Share of Top YouTube and Facebook Creators vs. Share of Views by Platform,” Global, Q2 2017, creators with 50M+ total views comprise 24% of the selected YouTube creators and account for 71% of...
Among top creators with over 50M views in Q2 2017, influencers account for 83% of YouTube views and media companies 17%; on Facebook, the split is 52% influencers and 48% media companies (p. 53).
The report identifies TV shows, artists, and TV networks among leading U.S. media-company creators on YouTube (p. 55).

findings.text: Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E. The page’s global consumer VR adoption chart measures users as a percentage of population, spans 2016–2021E, and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The chart labels the Mobile VR series with a footnote excluding Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers. It lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption.

evidence_spans.text: The page headline forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption. Its chart title specifies consumer VR adoption globally over 2016–2021E as a percentage of population, and the y-axis specifies users as a percentage of global population. Footnote 1 identifies the seventh-generation gaming-console modeling basis. The “Mobile VR²” series label is attached to the mobile line, and footnote 2 excludes Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers from that series. The mass-adoption barriers box lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area. The timeline marks 2016 without E and the 2017–2021 estimates with E.

findings.text: In Activate’s U.S. 2017 cord-cutter substitution chart, a higher share of sports viewers cited Broadcast than Virtual Pay TV (31% versus 21%); the same was true for non-sports viewers (21% versus 15%). Sports viewers watched more than five hours of sports programming per week, while non-sports viewers reported watching no sports programming on a regular basis.

findings.text: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, are reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours. Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, are reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours.
findings.statement: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, are reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours. Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, are reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours.

verified_facts.statement: Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E. The page’s global consumer VR adoption chart measures users as a percentage of population, spans 2016–2021E, and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The chart labels the Mobile VR series with a footnote excluding Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers. It lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption.
qualifiers: The chart shows 2016 without an E and labels 2017E–2021E as estimates.
The cardboard-viewer exclusion applies specifically to the Mobile VR series, not all VR adoption.
The page does not numerically define the threshold for “scaled” adoption.

source_truth_notes_by_page.42: The page headline forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption. Its chart title specifies consumer VR adoption globally over 2016–2021E as a percentage of population, and the y-axis specifies users as a percentage of global population. Footnote 1 identifies the seventh-generation gaming-console modeling basis. The “Mobile VR²” series label is attached to the mobile line, and footnote 2 excludes Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers from that series. The mass-adoption barriers box lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area. The timeline marks 2016 without E and the 2017–2021 estimates with E.

consumer-vr-adoption-outlook.statement: Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E. The page’s global consumer VR adoption chart measures users as a percentage of population, spans 2016–2021E, and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The chart labels the Mobile VR series with a footnote excluding Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers. It lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption.
qualifiers: The chart shows 2016 without an E and labels 2017E–2021E as estimates.
The cardboard-viewer exclusion applies specifically to the Mobile VR series, not all VR adoption.
The page does not numerically define the threshold for “scaled” adoption.

source_truth_notes_by_page.42: The page headline forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption. Its chart title specifies consumer VR adoption globally over 2016–2021E as a percentage of population, and the y-axis specifies users as a percentage of global population. Footnote 1 identifies the seventh-generation gaming-console modeling basis. The “Mobile VR²” series label is attached to the mobile line, and footnote 2 excludes Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers from that series. The mass-adoption barriers box lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area. The timeline marks 2016 without E and the 2017–2021 estimates with E.

findings.text: Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E. The page’s global consumer VR adoption chart measures users as a percentage of population, spans 2016–2021E, and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The chart labels the Mobile VR series with a footnote excluding Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers. It lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption.

Its chart title specifies consumer VR adoption globally over 2016–2021E as a percentage of population, and the y-axis specifies users as a percentage of global population. Footnote 1 identifies the seventh-generation gaming-console modeling basis. The “Mobile VR²” series label is attached to the mobile line, and footnote 2 excludes Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers from that series. The mass-adoption barriers box lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area. The timeline marks 2016 without E and the 2017–2021 estimates with E.

findings.text: In Activate’s U.S. 2017 cord-cutter substitution chart, a higher share of sports viewers cited Broadcast than Virtual Pay TV (31% versus 21%); the same was true for non-sports viewers (21% versus 15%). findings.text: In 2017, among news readers in the five selected countries, the share reporting perceived trustworthiness was higher for News Media than for Social Media: Canada 51% vs. 24%, Ireland 47% vs. 28%, the United Kingdom 41% vs. 18%, Australia 40% vs. 27%, and the United States 38% vs. 20%.

findings.text: In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, are reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours. Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, are reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours.

verified_facts.statement: Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E. The page’s global consumer VR adoption chart measures users as a percentage of population, spans 2016–2021E, and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The chart labels the Mobile VR series with a footnote excluding Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers. It lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption.
qualifiers: The chart shows 2016 without an E and labels 2017E–2021E as estimates.
The cardboard-viewer exclusion applies specifically to the Mobile VR series, not all VR adoption.
The page does not numerically define the threshold for “scaled” adoption.

source_truth_notes_by_page.42: The page headline forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption. Its chart title specifies consumer VR adoption globally over 2016–2021E as a percentage of population, and the y-axis specifies users as a percentage of global population. The “Mobile VR²” series label is attached to the mobile line, and footnote 2 excludes Google Cardboard and third-party cardboard viewers from that series. The mass-adoption barriers box lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area. The timeline marks 2016 without E and the 2017–2021 estimates with E.

issues.message: [family_confidence] Artifact family 'quotes' abstained at confidence=0.00 because quotes_missing.

[public_editorial_quality.semantic_review] The survey findings are correctly attributed to audience stages and sample sizes, but the text omits that the source page does not specify geography, a material boundary on the finding’s applicability.

[public_editorial_quality.semantic_review] The post calls the cohort only the “top 25% of users,” omitting the source’s defining criterion of 4.5+ hours of daily video attention. This blurs which users the reported shares describe.

[public_editorial_quality.source_limitation_omitted] The primary podcast insight omits the source’s explicit limitation that geography is not specified. Adding this qualification prevents readers from inferring geographic applicability beyond the source evidence. Dimensions: limitations: The primary podcast finding does not disclose that the source page specifies no geography, leaving its scope open to overgeneralization.
